subject: Banking
title: The Bulge Bracket Banks
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Bulge Bracket Banks usable.

hook.text: Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley. These are the bulge bracket, the largest and most prestigious investment banks.

buildup.text: The name comes from old tombstone ads in newspapers. The biggest banks' names literally bulged out in larger font.

discovery.text: Bulge bracket banks handle the largest deals globally.

twist.text: Before 2008, there were five major independent investment banks. Bear Stearns and Lehman Brothers collapsed.

climax.text: The financial crisis proved that even the most elite banks can fail. Size and prestige do not guarantee survival.

punchline.text: Five bulge bracket banks became three in 2008. Elite is not invincible.

quiz.question: Where does the term 'bulge bracket' come from?
options: Banks' names appearing in larger font on deal tombstone ads

details.summary: Bulge bracket banks are the largest global investment banks including Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, and Bank of America that dominate deal-making, underwriting, and trading with operations spanning every major market worldwide.
details.whyItMatters: A handful of bulge bracket banks control the majority of global M&A advisory, securities underwriting, and institutional trading. Their dominance shapes capital flows and determines which companies get funded and which deals get done.
takeaways: Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan, and Morgan Stanley lead the bulge bracket
These banks handle the largest and most complex global transactions
Bulge bracket status is determined by deal volume league table rankings

faq.question: What does bulge bracket mean?
faq.answer: The term comes from old tombstone advertisements for securities offerings, where the lead underwriter's name appeared in larger font that bulged out. Today it refers to the elite tier of global investment banks that consistently lead league tables.

faq.question: Are bulge bracket banks losing market share?
faq.answer: Independent advisory firms like Evercore, Lazard, and Centerview have gained share in M&A. But bulge brackets retain advantages in underwriting, trading, and lending that independents cannot match. The full-service model remains dominant.
